questions.scenario: A learner runs `git init` and then `git add .` in a Maven project that has already been built. The first commit contains the `target/` folder and IntelliJ's `.idea/` settings.
questions.question: What should they have done first?
options: Run `./mvnw clean` before every commit
Create a `.gitignore` listing `target/`, `.idea/` and similar files before the first `git add`
Use `git add *.java` only
Commit everything; GitHub removes build output automatically
questions.explanation: `.gitignore` stops build output and personal IDE files from being tracked. Generated files bloat the repository and cause pointless conflicts; the wrapper scripts and sources are what belong in Git.

questions.scenario: A developer commits `application.properties` containing a live payment-provider API key to a private GitHub repository, notices an hour later, and deletes the line in a new commit.
questions.question: What must they do now?
options: Nothing more; the latest commit no longer has the key
Rotate the key with the provider (issue a new one and revoke the old one), then move it to an environment variable
Make the repository private again
Rename the property
questions.explanation: Git keeps every version, so the key is still in history and must be treated as leaked. Rotating it is the real fix; cleaning history and moving secrets to environment variables come after.

questions.scenario: You edited three files and want to commit only the fix in `FeeCalculator.java`, leaving the other two changes for later.
questions.question: Which sequence does that?
options: `git commit -am "Fix fee rounding"`
`git add src/main/java/ng/itlearning/fees/FeeCalculator.java` then `git commit -m "Fix fee rounding"`
`git push` then `git commit`
`git restore .` then `git commit`
questions.explanation: Only staged changes go into a commit. `git commit -am` stages every modified tracked file; `git restore .` would discard all three changes.

questions.scenario: A commit pushed to `main` last week introduced a wrong fee, and other people have pulled `main` since then.
questions.question: What is the safest way to undo it?
options: `git revert <hash>`, which adds a new commit that reverses it, then push
Delete the repository and push a fresh copy
Edit the old commit's files directly on GitHub's history page
`git restore` the file and don't commit
questions.explanation: Revert adds history instead of rewriting it, so everyone's copies stay consistent and the audit trail shows both the mistake and the fix.

questions.scenario: Which commit message best follows good practice?
questions.question: Choose the best message.
options: `update`
`fixed some stuff in the fee code and also README`
`Reject transfers from frozen wallets`
questions.explanation: One logical change, described in the imperative mood, short enough for `git log --oneline`. It tells a reader in six months what changed and makes it easy to find.

questions.scenario: After merging a branch, a file contains lines starting with `<<<<<<< HEAD`, `=======` and `>>>>>>> add-pos-fee`.
questions.question: What do you do?
options: Commit the file as it is
Edit it to the correct final code, remove the three marker lines, run the tests, then `git add` and `git commit`
Delete the file
Run `git push --force`
questions.explanation: This is a merge conflict: both branches changed the same lines. You decide the correct result; the markers must never be committed, and the tests confirm the merge works.

questions.scenario: A project's GitHub Actions run fails at `./mvnw -B verify` with `Permission denied`, although the build works on the learner's Windows laptop.
questions.question: What is the likely cause and fix?
options: GitHub doesn't support Maven; switch to Gradle
The `mvnw` script isn't marked executable in Git; run `git update-index --chmod=+x mvnw` and commit
The repository must be public for Actions to run
Java 21 isn't available on GitHub runners
questions.explanation: Linux runners need the execute bit, which Windows doesn't record by default. Setting it in Git fixes it for every machine.

questions.scenario: A learner works alone on their capstone and pushes every change straight to `main` without running the tests.
questions.question: Which habit should they adopt, even working alone?
options: Push once a week instead
Work on a branch per change, push it, open a pull request, wait for green CI and review the diff before merging
Disable CI so `main` never shows red
Keep a second repository as a backup
questions.explanation: Branches and pull requests give a checked, reviewable path into `main`, which is how every team works and what interviewers and capstone assessors look for in your history.
